Log in here » BUDAPEST, Hungary (AP) — Hungary’s government announced an investigation Monday into a large foreign investment by Chinese automaker BYD negotiated by a former foreign minister who last week resigned from Parliament to take an executive position at the company. Péter Szijjártó’s announcement last Wednesday that he would take the job at the world’s top electric carmaker prompted accusations of a conflict of interest and criticism over his role in facilitating substantial government subsidies to the company while in office. Prime Minister Péter Magyar told lawmakers on Monday that Szijjártó, a close ally of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, had helped BYD while he was in office “with hundreds of billions (of forints) in public money, diplomatic support and state infrastructure.” Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar holds an extraordinary press briefing following a voting on the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law in the parliament building in Budapest, Hungary, Monday, July 13, 2026. (Tamas Purger/MTI via AP) “We will examine all the decisions, negotiations and state commitments made by Péter Szijjártó that were related to the BYD Hungary investment,” Magyar said Monday. He added the investigation would look into all subsidies, tax breaks, permits, environmental exemptions and publicly-funded investments given to large multinational firms during Orbán’s tenure. “We will investigate who made these decisions, who prepared them, what professional warnings were ignored, and how much burden they left on Hungarian taxpayers, workers, local communities and the environment,” Magyar said. Neither Szijjártó nor BYD have responded to Magyar’s allegations of conflict of interest while Szijjártó was in office. The former foreign minister has posed his new job as a “prestigious” opportunity to work for one the “greatest success stories” in the automotive industry. While serving in government, Szijjártó was instrumental in securing foreign investments in Hungary from Chinese companies, including his now-employer BYD, which received considerable state subsidies during his tenure. In 2023, Szijjártó announced that BYD would open its first European factory in Hungary — allowing the conglomerate to skirt European Union import tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles imposed to protect the continent’s domestic auto manufacturing sector. In 2025, Szijjártó also announced BYD would locate its European headquarters and a research and development center in Budapest and receive 20 billion forints ($63.7 million) in government assistance. The investments were part of the Orbán government’s push to make Hungary a global hub of lithium-ion battery manufacturing, largely through attracting Chinese battery manufacturers who opened a series of plants across the country. The moves led local residents, environmentalists and opposition politicians to protest over fears the new industry would exacerbate existing environmental problems, hit the country’s precious water supplies and further undermine its economy to China. While foreign minister, Szijjártó also maintained close relations with Russia despite its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022. Breaking with nearly all of his EU counterparts, he frequently traveled to Moscow to negotiate agreements on purchasing Russian oil and gas and to meet with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, whom he referred to as his “friend.” He was embroiled in controversy during Hungary’s 2026 election campaign when the Washington Post reported that he made regular phone calls to Lavrov during high-level EU meetings with “live reports on what’s been discussed.” Szijjártó has dismissed the report while acknowledging that he conferred with Lavrov before and after EU foreign minister meetings about their agenda and decisions. During a government news conference last week, Magyar said that “as far as I know,” an investigation had been launched concerning Szijjártó’s connections to the Russian government. Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP/Getty Images First Edition newsletter Israel-Gaza war Wednesday briefing: Inside sweeping UK sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements In today’s newsletter: Ed Miliband has announced the strongest statement on Israel’s actions ever issued by the the UK government, but will it make a meaningful difference to Palestinians? Hettie O'Brien Wed 9 Sep 2026 01.46 EDT Last modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. For almost half a century, British governments have condemned illegal Israeli settlements, acknowledging they represent an obstacle to peace and threaten the prospect of a two-state solution. And yet no government has ever compelled Israel to stop its expansion. Ed Miliband’s statement in the House of Commons yesterday was an attempt to change that. In a powerful and emotive speech, the foreign secretary recounted childhood memories of picking oranges on his grandmother’s kibbutz, accused Israeli “terrorists” of ethnic cleansing in the West Bank and announced a series of new measures intended to address what he described as a “deeply painful contrast” between rhetoric and reality. It was the strongest statement on Israel’s actions ever issued by the UK government. But will it make a difference to Palestinians living under the omnipresent threat of violence? Today’s newsletter, with the Guardian’s chief Middle East correspondent Emma-Graham Harrison and our diplomatic editor Patrick Wintour , drills into the details of Miliband’s announcement and explores that question. That’s after the headlines. Five big stories UK news | Police have been told by the government they expect better intelligence gathering after masked far-right groups took to the streets at the weekend, the Guardian has learned, as the Kent force admitted mishandling warnings of potential trouble. UK politics | Andy Burnham should tackle inequality in the UK by introducing a wealth tax, universal free personal social care and bringing gas and electricity networks under public ownership, according to a report from more than a dozen influential thinkers. Airline industry | Flight delays and cancellations were expected to continue today at UK airports after another air traffic control failure kept planes grounded for hours, affecting hundreds of thousands of passengers. Iran | Iranian forces claimed to have seized an American underwater drone in the strait of Hormuz that the US military said had “malfunctioned” more than a day earlier. US news | Donald Trump gave sizeable holiday gifts to four White House aides, according to new financial disclosures released by the administration, including $45,000 to executive assistant Natalie Harp. In depth: Could Miliband’s statement shift what seems politically possible? View image in fullscreen The Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim near the E1 corridor, where a housing project could cleave the West Bank in two. Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images The number of settlers in the occupied West Bank (including East Jerusalem) has risen from 270,000 in 1993 at the time of the Oslo Accords to about 770,000 today. Settlements are often framed as the project of violent extremists backed by far-right cabinet ministers, but Israel’s annexation enjoys longstanding cross-party support. As Emma Graham-Harrison wrote in January , the idea has “persisted in Israeli political imagination,” and although Israeli politicians have condemned settler violence, roughly half of Israelis think settlements help Israel’s security. In August, Benjamin Netanyahu’s government opened the tendering process for construction work on the E1 settlement, a vast project for 1,200 homes that would cut across the heart of the West Bank, dividing it in two and jeopardising the prospect of a two-state solution. Final bids for these contracts close days before the Israeli election next month, and the timing is strategic. “Netanyahu is trying to make E1 an election issue,” Patrick Wintour tells me. Miliband’s predecessors Yvette Cooper and David Lammy condemned the plans for E1, and Cooper backed international sanctions on individual settlers. But neither went as far as Miliband. “He’s a more decisive foreign secretary,” Patrick tells me. “You can’t sporadically say this is an outrage, and then not mention it for two months”. His stance also reflects Labour’s desire to win back voters on the left. The post-match analysis from Labour’s disastrous May local elections focused on the threat of Reform, but the Greens were a bigger threat to Labour’s vote. Miliband acknowledged yesterday that “Labour has not done enough in the face of what is happening”, and has announced these sanctions just before a pivotal byelection in Holborn and St Pancras, where the leader of the Green party, Zack Polanski, will be contesting Keir Starmer’s former seat. What has Miliband announced? It’s worth remembering where we were just two years ago, when Starmer’s government was still resisting calls for a ceasefire in Gaza. Although Starmer became more critical of Netanyahu’s government and ultimately recognised Palestinian statehood, Miliband’s speech marked a significant shift in tone and substance from this equivocating stance. He framed his intervention not as an argument with Israelis, “with whom the UK has unshakeable bonds”, but with the conduct of Israel’s government, its illegal occupation of Palestine , and with “settler terrorists”, while attacking the Boycott, Divest and Sanctions movement that calls to limit all trade with Israel. The first measure he announced is a widely anticipated ban on the import of goods from illegal settlements. This is important, not least because these settlements violate international law, but the economic impact of the ban will probably be minimal. The settlement economy is relatively small, and its products are already excluded from a 1995 EU free trade deal that reduces the tariffs on Israeli imports to Europe. It’s also kept alive by generous subsidies from the Israeli government. Israeli exporters to Europe regularly hide the origins of produce grow in settlements, something that could be dealt with by the “comprehensive sanctions regime” Miliband is working up with the business secretary. As significant as the ban itself is the fact France and Canada will join the UK in sanctioning Israeli settlements, a diplomatic coup for Miliband. Far-right ministers such as Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir have come out forcefully against Miliband’s sanctions (on Monday, Ben-Gvir issued a statement in Spanish calling for sanctions on Britain over its “occupation” of the Falkland Islands). Part of the reason is because Israel’s economy is bound far more closely to Europe than to the United States, and they fear a domino effect. “The UK is a permanent member of the security council, and they’re worried that Miliband’s statement could shift the window in terms of what seems politically possible,” says Emma. “Someone else stands up and says it, and suddenly, you aren’t taking an initiative – you’re following another country.” What will this mean for illegal settlements? One of its most transformative changes could be Miliband’s pledge to take action against companies and individuals who finance or “facilitate” illegal settlements. Any individual or company that wants to bid for government led construction projects, including new settlement expansion, needs a guarantor to underwrite their new property. Settlement residents also need banking services. Under these changes, banks and other companies that provide services to Israeli settlements will be sanctioned . “Hypothetically, this could force mainstream financial organisations in Israel to choose between financing settlements, or doing business with the UK,” Emma says. What has the fallout been? Israeli ministers have frequently made their intentions in the West Bank clear, but the gap between reality and the reactions of the international community is vast. Miliband’s statement went some way towards closing that. He announced that the British government officially views Israel’s occupation as unlawful (it had previously declared settlements illegal but remained silent on the wider occupation) and that it will refuse all licences for arms that contribute to the occupation. He chose his words carefully, accusing “settler terrorists” of “ethnic cleansing”. As the Israeli human rights lawyer Michael Sfard observed, the recognition of ethnic cleansing triggers legal obligations on the UK to prevent it in the West Bank, potentially dictating “many aspects of British policy towards Israel”. Israel retaliated by announcing it will be closing the consulate in Jerusalem and banning 11 MPs (on a list topped by Jeremy Corbyn) from entering the country. Meanwhile, the US has threatened “repercussions”. “There is no limit on what Trump could potentially do,” Patrick says. “But it’s worth bearing in mind that he is quite ambivalent about Netanyahu at the moment.” Their relationship has soured over Israel’s refusal to agree to Trump’s peace plan and the ongoing conflict in Iran. Unquestioning bipartisan support for Israel among US politicians appears to be faltering. Rahm Emanuel, Obama’s former chief of staff who is sounding out a presidential bid, has said he would back sanctions on companies financing illegal settlements. Earlier this week, Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, attacked Miliband for “Jew hate” over the (not yet announced) sanctions plans, but he has also called settler violence an “act of terror”. Miliband’s statement is a powerful recognition of the international law that Israel has relentlessly tried to reject, and comes at a time when itlooks increasingly isolated. What else we’ve been enjoying View image in fullscreen More than 480 private firms have been paid £250m for 1,800 unlawful placements of children over the past two years. Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images Tom Wall’s investigation reveals how councils are paying millions to house at-risk children in unsuitable care homes, including hotels, Airbnb properties and, in one case, a tent. It’s a tough read , but I’m grateful that Tom’s kept the spotlight on children, who need us most and who we, as a society, serve least. The front pages View image in fullscreen Photograph: The Guardian “UK condemns ‘ethnic cleansing by Israeli terrorists’ in West Bank”, is the Guardian ’s front page today. The Times leads with “Israel reacts with fury to UK curbs on settlements”, the i Paper also has “Israeli fury after UK accuses settlers of ethnic cleansing” and Metro runs “Backlash as UK accuses Israel”. The Mail says “Miliband accused of putting Jews in UK in danger”, and the Express writes “‘You have put an increased target on us’”. Elsewhere, the FT splashes “Bailey warns of ‘upside’ inflation risks as debt costs pile pressure on Healey”, the Telegraph writes “Air traffic collapse grounds flights”, and the Sun has “That’s another flyin’ mess”. The Latest Photograph: The Guardian UK condemns Israeli settlers conducting ethnic cleansing in West Bank The UK has attacked ‘settler terrorism’ deployed in a campaign of ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, while announcing sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in occupied Palestine. Foreign secretary Ed Miliband delivered the strongest condemnation of the actions of the Israeli government ever by a British government, including the disproportionate killings in Gaza of at least 70,000 people including 20,000 children. Lucy Hough speaks to chief Middle East correspondent Emma Graham-Harrison. Cartoon of the day | Ella Baron View image in fullscreen Illustration: Ella Baron/The Guardian The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad View image in fullscreen Bogotá has launched a number of initiatives to assist its ageing population. Photograph: Bogotá Bogotá is not the only city to face the challenges of a rapidly aging population but, with a fertility rate lower than Tokyo, the Colombian capital is taking a creative approach . As multigenerational homes become less common, the mayor opened “care blocks”, where caregivers can drop off a toddler or an elderly relative for a few hours. Reducing social isolation is key, so the city has started prescribing culture and nature-based activities. Last December, a seniors’ grand ball saw about 4,500 older people dancing to live salsa at the city’s Movistar arena. Bottom row, from left: Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara and Mykhailo Fedorov, ex-defence minister [Getty Images and AP Photo] By Mansur Mirovalev Published On 12 Oct 2026 12 Oct 2026 Kyiv, Ukraine – The White House wants Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy gone. “I think it’s ⁠⁠time for Ukraine to get a new president,” United States President Donald Trump told reporters on Saturday, claiming that Zelenskyy’s months-long strikes on Russian refineries had hurt global diesel supplies. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 Trump calls for Ukraine election, says Zelenskyy failed to end war list 2 of 4 Oval Office spat to public rebukes: A timeline of Trump-Zelenskyy ties list 3 of 4 Zelenskyy says Russia violated energy truce announced by Trump list 4 of 4 Ukraine’s Zelenskyy accuses Russia of violating Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ end of list But Trump’s wish is not Ukraine’s command. Even though Zelenskyy’s five-year presidential term expired in 2024, Ukraine’s constitution and martial law grant him a wartime extension. Many Ukrainians want their political establishment to be renewed, but are reluctant to see a presidential vote before the four-and-a-half year war is over. In response to Trump’s remarks, Zelenskyy proposed holding a vote if Russian President Vladimir Putin guaranteed a 60-day ceasefire. However, if the elections are held in the near future, who could compete with Zelenskyy? “If the elections are held fast, one of the former military [commanders] is Zelenskyy’s most probable rival,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera. Meanwhile, old political heavyweights such as former President Viktor Poroshenko, who lost the 2019 presidential vote to Zelenskyy, and former Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko, who is being investigated for corruption, do not stand a chance, he said. Valerii Zaluzhnyi: ‘Most probable alternative’ Ukraine’s former top general and current ambassador to the United Kingdom tops the lists of Zelenskyy’s rivals. “At least since 2023, and especially since 2024, after his resignation, the most probable alternative to Zelenskyy, his most dangerous competitor who can defeat him in the election is Valerii Zaluzhnyi,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. Advertisement Almost two-thirds of Ukrainians – 64 percent – trust him, according to an October 8 poll by the Rating Group, a Kyiv-based pollster, and only 25 percent “distrust” him. This trust is rooted in his 2022 military triumphs. After defending Kyiv in the early weeks of Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, Zaluzhnyi led counteroffensives that returned 40 percent of Russian-controlled territory to Ukraine. He was fired in 2023 after a long-anticipated summer counteroffensive yielded no results. Zaluzhnyi remains a man of mystery when it comes to the most pressing postwar matters. Burly and imposing, the 53-year-old is deliberately taciturn, leaving the public guessing about his views on Ukraine’s economic restoration, crippling demographic crisis or push to join the European Union. He does not take part in talk shows, barely talks to journalists and occasionally publishes opinion pieces with detailed analyses of war-related problems and general statements about securing lasting peace and security guarantees from Ukraine’s Western partners. Zelenskyy’s second chance? The former comedian was elected in 2019 with 73 percent of the vote, the highest result in Ukraine’s post-Soviet history. Despite a string of corruption scandals in his inner circle, the 48-year-old is popular enough to take another swing at a presidency. More than half of Ukrainians – 53 percent – trust him, although 40 percent do not, according to the Rating Group’s poll. However, Trump’s renewed animosity may benefit Zelenskyy again. Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has a troubled history with his US counterpart [File: Peter Dejong/AP] After his February 2025 row with Trump in the Oval Office, Zelenskyy’s approval ratings hit a wartime high of 67 percent. However, Zelenskyy may have ruined his own chances with his appointment policies. “He came to power under the slogans of resetting the power, of picking the most competent, not the most trusted” ministers or advisers, analyst Tyshkevych said. Kyrylo Budanov: Trusted by more than half of Ukrainians Lt. Gen. Kyrylo Budanov is the second most popular and charismatic military leader who has a shot at becoming Ukraine’s president. The 40-year-old former top military intelligence officer was appointed head of Zelenskyy’s administration in January. Budanov led daring operations against Russia, including a raid on Russian-annexed Crimea in 2016 to plant explosives at a military airfield. In 2020, Zelenskyy appointed him head of the defence ministry’s intelligence directorate (GUR), which became an aggressive, tech-driven special forces service. Advertisement The GUR’s sea drone attacks damaged Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, forcing it to retreat from annexed Crimea to the Russian port of Novorossiysk. Budanov is trusted by 53 percent of Ukrainians and mistrusted by 31 percent, according to the Rating Group’s poll. Mykhailo Fedorov: Young, popular, daring At 35, Fedorov is the youngest person on the list of potential presidents. He rose to fame after Zelenskyy appointed him minister of digital transformation in 2019, and managed to radically simplify bureaucratic procedures in the corruption-plagued nation. His ministry launched Diia, a smartphone app that lets users access more than 100 government services online. In January, Zelenskyy appointed Fedorov, who had zero military background, as defence minister in charge of logistics, budgets, reforms, anticorruption measures and deals to secure multibillion-dollar Western aid or loans. Fedorov cracked down on corruption schemes by making procurement of new weaponry, food and medical supplies more transparent. He radically boosted the number of drones that paralysed Russia’s supply routes, destroyed arms and fuel depots, oil refineries and air defence systems. He also increased the number of ground robots to supply food and ammunition and rescue wounded soldiers. But the reforms angered Oleksandr Syrsky, the actual commander-in-chief, who reportedly pushed for Fedorov’s dismissal in July. Fedorov’s supporters rallied throughout Ukraine for weeks, while his approval ratings soared from 35 percent in June to 65 percent in July, according to the Rating Group’s polls. However, in August he made an unpopular move saying Ukraine should hold a presidential vote, and his current approval stands at 38 percent. Yevhenii Khmara: Ukraine’s unknown defence minister The top five list ends with Yevhenii Khmara, a general who replaced Fedorov as defence minister. A relative unknown until his appointment in July, he is trusted by 29 percent of Ukrainians and distrusted by 16 percent. He was a career intelligence official with a low public profile, but another 43 percent of those polled did not know who he was, according to the survey. Low hopes for a foreign minister and an ex-president Numbers six and seven on the list are Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, a career diplomat who secured crucial support from Turkiye and Poland, and ex-president Poroshenko. Both are trusted by 24 percent of Ukrainians. But Poroshenko, who came to power in 2014 on an anti-corruption ticket but got involved in a graft scandal with overpriced spare parts for military equipment, holds a low popularity rating – 70 percent of those polled distrust him.
